prompt: On which thread does an Android app receive a tap on one of its buttons?

choices.text: Whichever processor core is free at the time
choices.why: Free cores do not take the app's events. Several cores help only when the app hands work to other threads itself.

choices.text: A thread the system creates for each touch
choices.why: No thread is created per touch; the touch is queued for the main thread, which the documentation describes step by step.

choices.text: The main thread, the same one that draws the screen
choices.why: Right. Android calls it the UI thread for exactly that reason: touches arrive on it and drawing happens on it.

choices.text: A background thread, so that drawing is never interrupted
choices.why: That is the arrangement people imagine, and it is the reverse of the real one: input and drawing share one thread.

prompt: Android's documentation gives two rules for its single-thread model. Which pair is it?

choices.text: Do not block it; touch the toolkit only from it
choices.why: Right. The first sends slow work away, the second makes its result come back.

choices.text: Use one thread per screen, and close it when the screen closes
choices.why: Screens do not get threads of their own; every screen is drawn by the one main thread.

choices.text: Run all work on the UI thread; keep each function short
choices.why: Short functions help, but disk and network can block in one short call. Slow work must leave the thread.

choices.text: Draw from a worker; read input on the main thread
choices.why: Drawing from a worker is exactly what the second rule forbids, because the toolkit is not thread-safe.

prompt: In a React Native app, the JavaScript thread is busy for half a second. What still works during it?

choices.text: A button whose pressed look is set in JavaScript
choices.why: That touch waits for the JavaScript thread, so the button stops answering, the documentation's own example.

choices.text: Timers set with setTimeout
choices.why: Timers run on the same JavaScript thread and wait for it like everything else there.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since the whole app runs on one thread
choices.why: A React Native app has two threads that matter, and the native main one is not the busy one here.

choices.text: Scrolling a ScrollView
choices.why: Right. The scroll happens on the native main thread, which is free.

prompt: Why can a Node.js program stand in for a phone's main thread in this lesson's experiment?

choices.text: Because Node.js uses the same graphics engine as Android
choices.why: Node.js draws nothing. The model is about the loop, not about graphics.

choices.text: Its loop runs one function at a time, so a long one stops timers
choices.why: Right. That one property carries over exactly; the rest of a phone does not.

choices.text: Because Node.js measures frames exactly as a display does
choices.why: Its timers wobble, as the idle run shows; the lesson says plainly that it is a model.

choices.text: Because phones run JavaScript on their main thread, as Node.js does
choices.why: Native apps run Kotlin or Swift there; only the shape of the loop is shared.

prompt: A phone's display refreshes 120 times a second. How many milliseconds does one frame get? Give two decimal places.
A frame's work runs 1 ms past its 16.67 ms slot. According to Android's documentation, what does the user see?

choices.text: The frame, shown 1 ms late
choices.why: That is the common picture and the documentation contradicts it: a late frame is not shown late.

choices.text: The previous picture for another whole slot; the frame is dropped
choices.why: Right. Missing the slot by any amount loses the frame.

choices.text: A blank screen until the work ends
choices.why: The screen keeps the last picture it had; nothing goes blank.

choices.text: The ANR dialog
choices.why: An ANR takes 5 seconds without answering input, not 1 ms.

prompt: Match how long a frame took to what Android's documentation calls it.
An animation's work takes 12 ms a frame and runs smoothly on a 60 Hz phone. On a 120 Hz phone, unchanged, what happens?

choices.text: It runs twice as smoothly, because the screen is faster
choices.why: A faster screen asks more often, which leaves each frame less time, not more.

choices.text: The system lowers the screen to 60 Hz for that app
choices.why: The lesson describes no such rescue; it says the frames are dropped.

choices.text: Nothing changes; the budget is 16 ms on every phone
choices.why: 16 ms is the budget at 60 Hz only. The budget is 1000 divided by the refresh rate.

choices.text: It misses slots: 12 ms is over the 8.33 ms budget
choices.why: Right. Code that fits at 60 Hz can miss every slot at 120 Hz.

prompt: Which frame is allowed to take longer than 16 ms without being a defect, according to the same Android page?

choices.text: The first frame of a new screen
choices.why: Right. The screen has to be built and laid out before it can be drawn.

choices.text: The last frame before the app goes to the background
choices.why: The page names no such exception.

choices.text: Any frame during a scroll
choices.why: Scrolling is exactly where a slow frame shows as a stutter.

choices.text: Every frame on a 120 Hz display
choices.why: A 120 Hz display gives less time, 8.33 ms, not an exemption.

prompt: Which of these, done on the main thread, can cost the planner frames? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Parsing a year of sessions downloaded as one JSON document
choices.why: Computing: the parser reads every character before it returns.

choices.text: Reading the saved plan from a file
choices.why: Waiting: storage answers in its own time while the thread does nothing.

choices.text: Fetching the course list from a server
choices.why: Waiting, and the longest kind: a network can take seconds or never answer.

choices.text: Setting a session's done flag in a plan of five sessions
choices.why: Copying a list of five takes far less than a frame; it is the size of the work that matters.

prompt: Why is a network call on the main thread a problem even though the processor is idle while it waits?

choices.text: Because the radio uses the processor while it waits
choices.why: The processor really is idle. The cost is the thread, not the processor.

choices.text: It is a problem only on iOS
choices.why: Android throws NetworkOnMainThreadException for it; both platforms treat it as a fault.

choices.text: While it waits, the loop cannot turn, so no frame is drawn
choices.why: Right. Waiting holds the thread exactly as computing does.

choices.text: Because a request from the main thread is sent twice, once per retry
choices.why: Nothing about the thread repeats the request.

prompt: Match each signal to the platform or tool it comes from.

pairs.right: Android, when a network connection is opened on the main thread
Android, a developer tool for accidental disk and network access
iOS, the code of a watchdog termination
Android, no answer to input within 5 seconds

right_distractors: React Native, a JavaScript thread that is busy for one frame

prompt: An iOS app holds its main thread far too long. What does the user see?

choices.text: The app is terminated by the watchdog and disappears
choices.why: Right. The crash report then carries the code 0x8badf00d.

choices.text: A dialog asking whether to wait or close the app
choices.why: That is Android's ANR dialog. iOS has none.

choices.text: A warning in the status bar
choices.why: There is no such warning; the watchdog terminates the app.

choices.text: Nothing; iOS moves the work to another thread for the app
choices.why: No system moves an app's work for it. That is the developer's job, and the next sections show how.

prompt: On Android, an ANR is triggered when the app has not responded to a touch or a key press within ___ seconds.
A React Native screen parses a large response with JSON.parse inside a press handler. A student says it is fine because fetch is asynchronous. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: JSON.parse runs on the native main thread, so the scroll freezes
choices.why: It runs on the JavaScript thread; the native scroll keeps going.

choices.text: Nothing; asynchronous code cannot block a thread
choices.why: Any synchronous step inside asynchronous code still runs to the end on its thread.

choices.text: The wait is asynchronous; the parse is synchronous and runs on the JavaScript thread
choices.why: Right. fetch frees the thread while the network answers, and JSON.parse holds it until it ends.

choices.text: fetch is synchronous in React Native
choices.why: fetch does not hold the thread while it waits; the problem is the parse.

prompt: In the lesson's main run, how many frames were dropped while the sort ran on the clock's thread?
In the captured runs, the sort took 554 ms on the main thread and 470 ms on the worker. What does the lesson conclude from that?

choices.text: Workers sort faster, so moving work makes it quicker
choices.why: The lesson says the difference does not matter: the work is the same, and the numbers vary from run to run.

choices.text: The work took about as long; what changed is which thread waited
choices.why: Right. With the worker, the clock drew a frame in every slot.

choices.text: The main thread is slower than a worker at sorting
choices.why: One run on one machine cannot show that, and the lesson does not claim it.

choices.text: The numbers prove the program has a bug
choices.why: Timings differ between runs; that is expected, and the lesson says so.

prompt: Why does frames.ts make its sessions from a fixed seed instead of Math.random?

choices.text: Math.random is not allowed in a worker
choices.why: It is allowed there. The reason is repeatability.

choices.text: To make the sort faster on both threads
choices.why: The seed changes which data is sorted, not how fast.

choices.text: Because type stripping refuses Math.random
choices.why: Type stripping only removes types; it refuses enums and namespaces, not functions.

choices.text: So both runs sort the same list
choices.why: Right. The worker makes its own copy, and the seed keeps it equal to the main thread's.

prompt: You run node frames.ts main on your laptop and get 41 frames dropped rather than 33. What does that tell you?

choices.text: That your file differs from the lesson's
choices.why: The same file gives different timings on another machine and on another run.

choices.text: That the Node.js you run is the wrong version
choices.why: A wrong version fails to run the file at all, as lesson 1 shows; it does not change a count.

choices.text: That run's sort took longer; the shape holds
choices.why: Right. Timings vary by machine and run; what holds is that the main run drops frames and the worker run does not.

choices.text: That the worker run will now drop frames as well
choices.why: The worker run keeps the clock's thread free whatever the machine's speed.

prompt: Put the three steps of moving work off the main thread in order.
items: Hand the slow work to another thread
Keep drawing frames on the main thread while it runs
Bring the result back to the main thread and show it

prompt: Match each Kotlin dispatcher to the work Android's documentation gives it.
right_distractors: drawing views from a background thread

prompt: In the Swift fragment, what does @MainActor on refresh() guarantee?

choices.text: That week is set on the main thread
choices.why: Right. The caller is on the main actor, so the result lands there.

choices.text: That the sort runs on the main thread
choices.why: The sort is inside Task.detached, which belongs to no actor; that is the point.

choices.text: That the function finishes within one frame
choices.why: No annotation can promise a duration; it says where code runs.

choices.text: That the work runs on a new thread created for it
choices.why: @MainActor means the main thread, the opposite of a new one.

prompt: A Kotlin worker thread finishes sorting and sets the list on screen directly from that thread. Which rule does it break?

choices.text: Do not block the UI thread
choices.why: It kept the UI thread free; that half was right.

choices.text: Use Dispatchers.IO for every background task
choices.why: There is no such rule; Default suits a sort.

choices.text: None; the toolkit accepts changes from any thread
choices.why: Android's documentation says the toolkit is not thread-safe.

choices.text: Do not touch the UI toolkit from outside the UI thread
choices.why: Right. The result has to come back to the main thread first: the third step.

prompt: The planner's week view stutters when it opens on a phone with a long history. The sort runs inside the function that draws the list. What is the first change?

choices.text: Lower the screen's refresh rate to 60 Hz
choices.why: A bigger budget hides the cost on one phone; the work is still on the drawing thread.

choices.text: Sort once, off the main thread
choices.why: Right. It leaves the drawing function and stops repeating on every draw, Android's ANR guide's own example.

choices.text: Show the ANR dialog earlier
choices.why: The app does not show that dialog; the system does, and it is the failure, not a fix.

choices.text: Turn on StrictMode in the release build
choices.why: StrictMode finds disk and network on the main thread during development; it does not move a sort.

prompt: Which of these is a good reason to run work on the main thread?

choices.text: It is a network request, and the answer is needed on screen
choices.why: The answer can come back to the main thread; the waiting must not happen there.

choices.text: It changes a view, and it is quick
choices.why: Right. Touching the UI is the main thread's job, and quick work fits in the frame.

choices.text: It runs once a day
choices.why: A frame lost once a day is still lost, and a long wait still earns an ANR.

choices.text: The phone has several cores, so the main thread is never full
choices.why: Cores do not share the main thread's work; it is one thread whatever the processor.

prompt: A frame that misses its slot by a single millisecond is not shown late; Android ___ it entirely.
